# "?" for a line in another form, a host that isn't a plain host name, or
# more than one line: nothing starts.
internet=$(awk "$awk_lib"'
  fenceline($0) { next }
  fence { next }
  /^## / { sec = (!seen && $0 ~ /^## Controls([ \t]|$)/); if (sec) seen = 1; next }
  sec && tolower($0) ~ /^[ \t]*([-*+][ \t]*)?(\*\*)?[ \t]*internet/ { n++; line = $0 }
  END {
    if (!n) { print "no"; exit }
    if (n > 1 || line !~ /^- Internet: \*\*/) { print "?"; exit }
    v = substr(line, length("- Internet: **") + 1); k = index(v, "**")
    if (k < 2) { print "?"; exit }
    print substr(v, 1, k - 1)
  }
' "$roadmap")
hosts=()
if [[ "$internet" == "shell only" ]]; then
  internet="shell"
elif [[ "$internet" != no && "$internet" != yes && "$internet" != "?" ]]; then
  for h in "${(@s:,:)internet}"; do
    h="${h//[[:space:]]/}"
    if [[ "$h" =~ '^(\*\.)?[A-Za-z0-9-]+(\.[A-Za-z0-9-]+)+(:[0-9]+)?$' ]]; then hosts+=("$h"); else internet="?"; break; fi
  done
  [[ "$internet" == "?" ]] || internet="hosts"
fi
case "$internet" in
  no)    internet_says="no: no web tools, and shell commands run sandboxed with no host allowed" ;;
  yes)   internet_says="yes: no sandbox, web tools as Orlando's own settings say" ;;
  hosts) internet_says="only ${(j:, :)hosts}, for shell commands; no web tools" ;;
  shell) internet_says="shell only: no web tools, and shell commands run outside the sandbox as before" ;;
  *)     internet_says="?" ;;
esac
unclear_internet='roadmap.md'"'"'s Internet line can'"'"'t be read: nothing starts. Write "- Internet: **no**", "- Internet: **shell only**", "- Internet: **yes**", or the hosts a lead'"'"'s commands may reach, such as "- Internet: **registry.npmjs.org, pypi.org**", once, or leave the line out for no.'
# Where a lead's settings are written when it has no internet or a list of
# hosts: under ~/.claude, which a sandboxed command can't write. Tests move it.
settings_dir="${RELAY_SETTINGS_DIR:-$HOME/.claude/relay-settings}"

# How a lead's process is told apart, by its command line. On the plan:
# "claude --remote-control <its name> ...". An older lead on the key: "claude
# --name <its name> ...". On sdk: "uv run <this folder>/sdk-run.py ...
# --label <its name> ...", the uv process being the pane's own program. Each
# is followed by "<Name>: Batch N". Two groups: the batch number is \3.
lead_re='^([^ ]*claude --(remote-control|name) |[^ ]*uv run [^ ]*sdk-run\.py .*--label )'

state="${found%% *}"
batch=$(print -r -- "${found#* }" | sed -E 's/^### (Batch [0-9]+).*/\1/')
number="${batch#Batch }"
sess="$name: $batch"

# This script's own ancestors: a lead that calls it is one of them.
ancestors=()
pid=$$
while [[ -n "$pid" && "$pid" != "1" && "$pid" != "0" ]]; do
  ancestors+=("$pid")
  pid=$(ps -o ppid= -p "$pid" 2>/dev/null | tr -d ' ')
done
# The status word of a batch, by its number: queued, running, done.
status_of() {
  awk -v n="$1" "$awk_lib"'
    fenceline($0) { on = 0; next }
    fence { next }
    /^[ \t]*>/ { on = 0; next }
    /^## / { batches = (!seen && $0 ~ /^## Batches([ \t]|$)/); if (batches) seen = 1; on = 0; next }
    { if (on && $0 ~ /^Status: /) { s = $0; sub(/^Status: \*\*/, "", s); sub(/\*\*.*/, "", s); print s; exit }
      on = (batches && $0 ~ ("^### Batch " n "([^0-9]|$)")) }
  ' "$roadmap"
}
# Is a lead of this relay the one calling? Then which batch is its own, and
# whether that batch is done. A lead whose batch is done has ended its work,
# so its pane is put away below whatever else happens.
caller_batch=""
for a in "${ancestors[@]}"; do
  n=$(ps -o args= -p "$a" 2>/dev/null | sed -n -E "s/${lead_re}$name: Batch ([0-9]+)([^0-9].*)?$/\3/p" | head -1)
  if [[ -n "$n" ]]; then caller_batch="$n"; fi
done
caller_done=0
if [[ -n "$caller_batch" && "$(status_of "$caller_batch")" == done ]]; then caller_done=1; fi
# Other lead sessions of this project. One whose batch is marked done has
# finished and is only an open pane, waiting to be put away: it is not
# leading anything, and doesn't count.
others=()
finished=()
finished_pids=()
for other in $(pgrep -f "${lead_re}$name: Batch [0-9]+" || true); do
  (( ${ancestors[(Ie)$other]} )) && continue
  n=$(ps -o args= -p "$other" 2>/dev/null | sed -n -E "s/${lead_re}$name: Batch ([0-9]+)([^0-9].*)?$/\3/p" | head -1)
  if [[ -n "$n" && "$(status_of "$n")" == done ]]; then
    finished+=("Batch $n")
    finished_pids+=("$other")
  else
    others+=("$other")
  fi
done

rex_bin=$(command -v rex || true)
[[ -n "$rex_bin" ]] || rex_bin="$HOME/Library/Application Support/com.superlogical.rex/RexServer/Versions/Current/Rex Server.app/Contents/MacOS/rex"
# jq (part of macOS) reads what Rex says about its panes. Without it sessions
# still start, but their tab isn't named and stray finished panes aren't found.
jq_bin=$(command -v jq || true)
# How long a finished pane must be idle before it closes. Tests shorten it.
close_after="${RELAY_CLOSE_AFTER:-900}"

# pane_of <process id>: the Rex pane that process runs in. Rex knows each
# pane's program by its process id. Sets REPLY to the pane's block id.
pane_of() {
  REPLY=""
  [[ -x "$rex_bin" && -n "$jq_bin" ]] || return 1
  local s b p
  for s in $("$rex_bin" ls --json --autostart=false 2>/dev/null | "$jq_bin" -r '.sessions[]?.session_id' 2>/dev/null); do
    for b in $("$rex_bin" block ls -s "$s" --json --autostart=false 2>/dev/null | "$jq_bin" -r '.blocks[]?.block_id' 2>/dev/null); do
      p=$("$rex_bin" block call -b "$b" process --autostart=false 2>/dev/null | "$jq_bin" -r '.child.pid // empty' 2>/dev/null) || p=""
      if [[ "$p" == "$1" ]]; then REPLY="$b"; return 0; fi
    done
  done
  return 1
}

# pane_state <process id>: what that lead's pane reports, for --status:
# "working", "idle for 2 h 10 min", or nothing when it can't be read. Read the
# same way close-pane-later.sh reads it. Sets REPLY, and LEAD_IDLE to the idle
# seconds (0 when working or unknown).
pane_state() {
  REPLY="" LEAD_IDLE=0
  pane_of "$1" || return 1
  local st count working last at idle
  st=$("$rex_bin" block call -b "$REPLY" program_status --autostart=false 2>/dev/null) || { REPLY=""; return 1; }
  REPLY=""
  print -r -- "$st" | "$jq_bin" -r '[.records[]?] as $r | "\($r | length) \([$r[] | select(.state == "working")] | length) \([$r[] | .updated_at // empty] | max // "")"' 2>/dev/null | read -r count working last
  [[ "$count" == <-> ]] && (( count > 0 )) || return 1
  if (( working > 0 )); then REPLY="working"; return 0; fi
  zmodload zsh/datetime
  [[ -n "$last" ]] && strftime -r -s at '%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S' "${last[1,19]}" 2>/dev/null || return 1
  idle=$(( EPOCHSECONDS - at ))
  (( idle >= 0 )) || return 1
  LEAD_IDLE=$idle
  if (( idle >= 3600 )); then REPLY="idle for $(( idle / 3600 )) h $(( idle % 3600 / 60 )) min"
  else REPLY="idle for $(( idle / 60 )) min"; fi
  return 0
}

if [[ "$mode" == status ]]; then
  echo "$name ($project)"
  awk "$awk_lib"'
    fenceline($0) { next }
    fence { next }
    /^## / { sec = (!seen && $0 ~ /^## Controls([ \t]|$)/); if (sec) seen = 1; next }
    sec && /^- (Relay|Stop after batch|Agents|Lead):/ { s = $0; sub(/^- /, "  ", s); gsub(/\*\*/, "", s); print s }
  ' "$roadmap"
  if [[ "$billing" == "?" ]]; then echo "  Billing: can't be read"; else echo "  Billing: $billing_says"; fi
  if [[ "$internet" == "?" ]]; then echo "  Internet: can't be read"; else echo "  Internet: $internet_says"; fi
  echo "Batches:"
  awk "$awk_lib"'
    fenceline($0) { name = ""; next }
    fence { next }
    /^[ \t]*>/ { name = ""; next }
    /^## / { batches = (!seen && $0 ~ /^## Batches([ \t]|$)/); if (batches) seen = 1; name = ""; next }
    { if (name != "" && $0 ~ /^Status: /) { s = $0; gsub(/\*\*/, "", s); sub(/^Status: /, "", s); print "  " name ": " s }
      name = (batches && $0 ~ /^### Batch [0-9]+/) ? substr($0, 5) : "" }
  ' "$roadmap"
  if (( ${#others} )); then
    # Each live lead, with what its pane reports. A lead stopped by a usage
    # limit in the middle of a turn stays alive and idle, and blocks every
    # restart until it is told to carry on or its pane is closed.
    running=() long_idle=0
    for o in "${others[@]}"; do
      r=$(ps -o args= -p "$o" 2>/dev/null | sed -n -E "s/${lead_re}($name: Batch [0-9]+)([^0-9].*)?$/\3/p" | head -1)
      [[ -n "$r" ]] || r="process $o"
      if pane_state "$o" && [[ -n "$REPLY" ]]; then r="$r ($REPLY)"; (( LEAD_IDLE >= 3600 )) && long_idle=1; fi
      running+=("$r")
    done
    echo "A lead session is running: ${(j:, :)running}"
    if (( long_idle )); then echo "A lead idle this long may have stopped at a usage limit, and blocks every restart. See \"After a crash, a power cut or a usage limit\" in the relay skill."; fi
  else
    echo "No lead session is running."
  fi
  if (( ${#finished} )); then echo "Finished, with its pane still open: ${(j:, :)finished}"; fi
  if [[ -n "$found" ]]; then echo "Next to lead: $batch ($state)"; else echo "Nothing is running or queued."; fi
  if [[ "$(relay_state)" == unclear ]]; then echo "$unclear_relay"; fi
  [[ -n "$unreadable_batches" ]] && echo "$unreadable_batches"
  [[ "$stop_after" == "?" ]] && echo "$unclear_stop"
  if [[ "$lead_says" == "?" ]]; then echo "$unclear_lead"; else echo "A new lead starts on: $lead_says."; fi
  [[ "$billing" == "?" ]] && echo "$unclear_billing"
  [[ "$billing" == api ]] && echo "$refused_api"
  [[ "$billing" == sdk && "$budget" == "?" ]] && echo "$unclear_budget"
  [[ "$internet" == "?" ]] && echo "$unclear_internet"
  if pgrep -f 'memory-fuse\.sh watch$' >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    echo "The memory fuse is watching."
  else
    echo "The memory fuse is not watching. It starts with the next lead."
  fi
  exit 0
fi

# close_later <block id>: closes that pane once its session has been idle
# long enough. The timer runs on its own, in no pane, one to a pane.
close_later() {
  if pgrep -f "close-pane-later.sh $1 " >/dev/null 2>&1; then return 0; fi
  ( "$here/close-pane-later.sh" "$1" "$close_after" </dev/null >/dev/null 2>&1 & )
}

# Finished leads whose panes are still open (a lead that ended without
# running this script, or whose timer was lost) are put away too.
sweep_finished() {
  local p
  for p in "${finished_pids[@]}"; do
    if pane_of "$p" && [[ "$REPLY" != "$REX_BLOCK" ]]; then close_later "$REPLY"; fi
  done
  return 0
}

# The pane this was run from, when a lead whose batch is done is the one
# calling, or --close-me was given.
close_caller() {
  [[ "$mode" == start && -n "$REX_BLOCK" && -x "$rex_bin" ]] || return 0
  (( close_me || caller_done )) || return 0
  close_later "$REX_BLOCK"
  echo "This session's pane closes by itself once it has been idle for $(( (close_after + 59) / 60 )) minutes. Write your last message to Orlando now, and do nothing else afterwards."
}

# What a real run ends with, whether or not anything was started.
put_away() {
  [[ "$mode" == start ]] || return 0
  sweep_finished
  close_caller
}

if [[ -n "$unreadable_batches" ]]; then
  echo "$unreadable_batches"
  put_away
  exit 0
fi
if [[ -z "$found" ]]; then
  echo "No batch is running or queued in roadmap.md: nothing to start."
  put_away
  exit 0
fi
case "$(relay_state)" in
  on) ;;
  unclear)
    echo "$unclear_relay"
    put_away
    exit 0 ;;
  *)
    echo "roadmap.md says the relay is off: nothing started."
    put_away
    exit 0 ;;
esac
if [[ "$stop_after" == "?" ]]; then
  echo "$unclear_stop"
  put_away
  exit 0
fi
if [[ "$state" == queued && "$stop_after" == <-> && "$number" -gt "$stop_after" ]]; then
  echo "roadmap.md says to stop after batch $stop_after: nothing started."
  put_away
  exit 0
fi
# Never two lead sessions for one project at once. The session that has just
# finished the batch before is still running when it calls this: it is one of
# this script's ancestors, and doesn't count.
if (( ${#others} )); then
  echo "Another lead session for $name is already running (process ${others[1]}): nothing started."
  close_caller
  exit 0
fi
# Nor a second session for a batch whose own lead is the one calling: it
# marks its batch done before it starts the next. With --close-me it is
# stopping part way, and only wants its pane put away.
if [[ "$state" == running && -n "$caller_batch" && "$caller_batch" == "$number" ]]; then
  if (( close_me )); then
    echo "$batch is marked running and this session is leading it: nothing started. The next start carries on from what is in the files."
    close_caller
  else
    echo "$batch is marked running and this session is leading it: nothing started. Mark it done in roadmap.md first."
  fi
  exit 0
fi

if [[ "$lead_says" == "?" ]]; then
  echo "$unclear_lead"
  put_away
  exit 0
fi
if [[ "$billing" == "?" ]]; then
  echo "$unclear_billing"
  put_away
  exit 0
fi
if [[ "$billing" == api ]]; then
  echo "$refused_api"
  put_away
  exit 0
fi
if [[ "$billing" == sdk && "$budget" == "?" ]]; then
  echo "$unclear_budget"
  put_away
  exit 0
fi
if [[ "$internet" == "?" ]]; then
  echo "$unclear_internet"
  put_away
  exit 0
fi

# The lead's settings. With internet: lead-settings.json as it is. Shell
# only: lead-settings.json and lead-offline.json's two denied web tools.
# Without, or with a list of hosts: lead-settings.json and lead-offline.json together,
# with the hosts, and each command in lead-offline.json's excludedCommands
# also written with the home folder spelled out, since a lead may type it
# either way. Those few commands run outside the sandbox: start-lead.sh, which
# drives Rex through its socket to start the next lead, and the /usage reader,
# which asks Claude Code. Written fresh at every start, so an edit to the file
# lasts only until then. A lead whose settings can't be put together doesn't
# start.
lead_settings="$skill/lead-settings.json"
if [[ "$internet" != yes ]]; then
  slug="${${(L)name}// /-}"
  lead_settings="$settings_dir/$slug.json"
  json=""
  if [[ -n "$jq_bin" ]]; then
    json=$("$jq_bin" -nc --slurpfile base "$skill/lead-settings.json" --slurpfile off "$skill/lead-offline.json" --arg home "$HOME" '
      if $shell == "1" then $base[0] | .permissions.deny = ((.permissions.deny // []) + $off[0].permissions.deny)
      else ($base[0] * $off[0])
        | .sandbox.network.allowedDomains = $ARGS.positional
        | .sandbox.excludedCommands += [.sandbox.excludedCommands[] | select(test("~/")) | gsub("~/"; $home + "/")]
      end
    ' --arg shell "$([[ $internet == shell ]] && print 1 || print 0)" --args "${hosts[@]}" 2>/dev/null) || json=""
  fi
  if [[ -z "$json" ]]; then
    echo "The lead's settings could not be put together from lead-settings.json and lead-offline.json (is jq there?): nothing starts." >&2
    exit 1
  fi
fi
# write_settings: puts them where the lead reads them, just before it starts.
write_settings() {
  [[ "$internet" == yes ]] && return 0
  /bin/mkdir -p "$settings_dir" && print -r -- "$json" > "$lead_settings.tmp" && /bin/mv -f "$lead_settings.tmp" "$lead_settings" && return 0
  echo "Could not write the lead's settings to $lead_settings: nothing starts." >&2
  exit 1
}

# RELAY_TEST_CLAUDE puts a stand-in in claude's place, for this script's own tests.
claude_bin="${RELAY_TEST_CLAUDE:-$HOME/.local/bin/claude}"
[[ -x "$claude_bin" ]] || claude_bin=$(command -v claude || true)
[[ -n "$claude_bin" ]] || { echo "Can't find the claude command." >&2; exit 1; }
[[ -x "$rex_bin" ]] || { echo "Can't find rex: the relay starts its sessions in Rex panes." >&2; exit 1; }

# The prompt is one plain line, so no shell on the way can mangle it.
prompt="Read $skill/lead.md and do what it says."
carrying=""
[[ "$state" == running ]] && carrying=" It carries on from where the stopped session left $batch."
opening=("$rex_bin" run --json --focus=false --label "$sess" -c "$project")
# lead-settings.json turns a permission question into a "no", so a lead never
# waits all night on one (Orlando's call). Leads only: his own
# sessions still ask. Without internet it comes with lead-offline.json, put
# together above.
session_cmd=(-- "$claude_bin" --remote-control "$sess" --permission-mode auto --settings "$lead_settings" "${lead_flags[@]}" "$prompt")
# On sdk: the same first message, model, effort, settings file and
# permission mode, through sdk-run.py, which may read this skill's folder
# (lead.md, the briefs) without asking, and loads the user's, project's and
# local settings too (their deny rules hold) and stops at the budget. The
# lead's agents run in its process, so they bill the key too. A lead stopped
# by its budget gets an entry in roadmap.md's Log from sdk-run.py.
# RELAY_TEST_UV puts a stand-in in uv's place, for this script's own tests.
if [[ "$billing" == sdk ]]; then
  uv_bin="${RELAY_TEST_UV:-$(command -v uv || true)}"
  [[ -n "$uv_bin" ]] || uv_bin="$HOME/.local/bin/uv"
  [[ -x "$uv_bin" ]] || { echo "Can't find uv: an sdk lead runs with uv run." >&2; exit 1; }
  session_cmd=(-- "$uv_bin" run "$here/sdk-run.py" --cwd "$project" --budget "$budget" --settings "$lead_settings" --read-dir "$skill" --roadmap "$roadmap" "${lead_flags[@]}" --label "$sess" --prompt "$prompt")
fi

if [[ "$mode" == dry-run ]]; then
  echo "Would start: $sess.$carrying"
  echo "On: $lead_says."
  [[ "$billing" == sdk ]] && echo "Billing: $billing_says."
  echo "Internet: $internet_says."
  [[ "$internet" != yes ]] && echo "Settings, written to $lead_settings at the start: $json"
  printf '%q ' "${opening[@]}" ${REX_SESSION:+-s} ${REX_SESSION:+"$REX_SESSION"} "${session_cmd[@]}"; echo
  exit 0
fi

# Where the new pane goes. Beside the lead that is handing over (the caller),
# or beside a finished lead's pane that is still open, so the relay keeps its
# tab. With neither, a new tab: in this Rex session if there is one, in Rex's
# default place otherwise.
write_settings
anchor=""
if [[ -n "$caller_batch" && -n "$REX_BLOCK" ]]; then
  anchor="$REX_BLOCK"
else
  for p in "${finished_pids[@]}"; do
    if pane_of "$p"; then anchor="$REPLY"; break; fi
  done
fi
out=""
started=0
if [[ -n "$anchor" ]]; then
  if out=$("${opening[@]}" --split=right -b "$anchor" "${session_cmd[@]}" 2>&1); then started=1; fi
fi
if (( ! started )); then
  if [[ -n "$REX_SESSION" ]] && out=$("${opening[@]}" -s "$REX_SESSION" "${session_cmd[@]}" 2>&1); then
    :
  elif out=$("${opening[@]}" "${session_cmd[@]}" 2>&1); then
    :
  else
    echo "Rex could not start the session: $out" >&2
    exit 1
  fi
fi
# The new pane's id. A split's answer also names the pane it was split from
# (its anchor), which is not the one wanted.
block=""
if [[ -n "$jq_bin" ]]; then
  block=$(print -r -- "$out" | "$jq_bin" -r '.block_ids[0] // empty' 2>/dev/null) || block=""
fi
if [[ -z "$block" ]]; then
  block=$(print -r -- "$out" | grep -v '"anchor_id"' | sed -n -E 's/.*"(block:[^"]+)".*/\1/p' | head -1)
fi

# Name the relay's tab after the session leading now, so Orlando can tell his
# tabs apart. A name he gave the tab himself is left alone.
name_tab() {
  [[ -n "$jq_bin" && -n "$block" ]] || return 0
  local info s w label
  info=$("$rex_bin" block inspect "$block" --json 2>/dev/null) || return 0
  s=$(print -r -- "$info" | "$jq_bin" -r '.session_id // empty' 2>/dev/null) || return 0
  w=$(print -r -- "$info" | "$jq_bin" -r '.block.window_id // empty' 2>/dev/null) || return 0
  [[ -n "$s" && -n "$w" ]] || return 0
  label=$("$rex_bin" window ls -s "$s" --json 2>/dev/null | "$jq_bin" -r --arg w "$w" '.windows[]? | select(.window_id == $w) | .label // empty' 2>/dev/null) || label=""
  if [[ -z "$label" || "$label" =~ '^Window [0-9a-f]+$' || "$label" == "$name: Batch "* ]]; then
    "$rex_bin" window rename "$w" "$sess" -s "$s" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
  fi
  return 0
}
name_tab

# Did it come up? Its process should be there within a few seconds.
up=0
for i in {1..20}; do
  for p in $(pgrep -f "${lead_re}$sess( |\$)" || true); do
    (( ${ancestors[(Ie)$p]} )) || up=1
  done
  (( up )) && break
  sleep 1
done
if (( ! up )); then
  echo "The session for $batch did not come up. Look at its pane: rex capture -b $block" >&2
  exit 1
fi
if [[ "$billing" == sdk ]]; then
  echo "Started a fresh session for $batch through the Agent SDK, billed to the API key, at most \$$budget. It is in this relay's tab in Rex as \"$sess\", and not in the Claude app: Remote Control needs the plan. Its cost goes to ~/.claude/sdk-costs.log.$carrying"
else
  echo "Started a fresh session for $batch. It is in this relay's tab in Rex and in the Claude app, both as \"$sess\".$carrying"
fi
echo "Read its pane with: rex capture -b $block"

# The memory fuse: one for the whole Mac while any relay lead runs. It stops a
# single runaway process that a lead or its agents started, before macOS runs
# out of memory. It runs on its own, in no pane, and ends by itself once no
# lead is left. A second one ends at once. A run with a stand-in for claude
# (this script's own tests) starts none.
if [[ -z "${RELAY_TEST_CLAUDE:-}" && -x "$here/memory-fuse.sh" ]]; then
  ( "$here/memory-fuse.sh" watch </dev/null >/dev/null 2>&1 & )
fi

# Put the finished sessions away, so old ones don't pile up for Orlando to
# close by hand. What each did is in roadmap.md's Log and in git.
put_away
````

### `watch-relay.zsh`

Watches one relay from another session and exits with an "EVENT:" line when a batch finishes, no lead is running, the relay's sessions have been quiet for 30 minutes, or a time limit passes. It costs nothing while it waits.

**Needs to run:** zsh, and the start script from this skill.

```
#!/bin/zsh
# Watches one relay and exits when something needs a look. It costs nothing while it waits.
# Usage: watch-relay.zsh <project folder> [minutes before it stops waiting]
# It prints a line starting "EVENT:" and exits when:
#   - a batch has been marked done since it started watching
#   - no lead session is running
#   - the relay's sessions have written nothing for 30 minutes
#   - the time limit passes
emulate -L zsh
repo=${1:?project folder}
limit_min=${2:-300}
script=$HOME/.claude/skills/relay/scripts/start-lead.sh
projects=$HOME/.claude/projects
pattern="*${repo:h:t}-${repo:t}*"

relay_status() { "$script" "$repo" --status 2>&1 }
count_done() { print -r -- "$1" | grep -c ': done' }
session_dirs() { find "$projects" -maxdepth 1 -type d -name "$pattern" }

start=$(date +%s)
first=$(relay_status)
done_start=$(count_done "$first")
watch_quiet=yes
[[ -z "$(session_dirs)" ]] && watch_quiet=no
print -r -- "Watching since $(date '+%a %H:%M'). Batches done at start: $done_start. Quiet check: $watch_quiet."

while true; do
  sleep 300
  out=$(relay_status)
  stamp=$(date '+%a %H:%M')
  if (( $(count_done "$out") > done_start )); then
    print -r -- "EVENT: a batch finished ($stamp)"; print -r -- "$out"; exit 0
  fi
  if ! print -r -- "$out" | grep -q 'A lead session is running'; then
    print -r -- "EVENT: no lead session is running ($stamp)"; print -r -- "$out"; exit 0
  fi
  if [[ $watch_quiet == yes ]]; then
    recent=$(session_dirs | while read -r d; do find "$d" -type f -mmin -30 -print -quit; done 2>&1 | head -1)
    if [[ -z "$recent" ]]; then
      print -r -- "EVENT: the relay's sessions have written nothing for 30 minutes ($stamp)"; print -r -- "$out"; exit 0
    fi
  fi
  if (( ( $(date +%s) - start ) / 60 >= limit_min )); then
    print -r -- "EVENT: time limit of $limit_min minutes ($stamp)"; print -r -- "$out"; exit 0
  fi
done
```

Previous: [Heartbeat](https://oneillo.com/ai-setup/skills/heartbeat/).
Next: [Rex](https://oneillo.com/ai-setup/skills/rex/).

# Evals

- Kind: Claude Code skill
- Address: https://oneillo.com/ai-setup/skills/evals/
- Last updated: 2026-11-27

> AI-written and cleaned from one person's working setup. Placeholders in angle brackets are not real values: ask your user for theirs. The newest version is at https://oneillo.com/ai-setup/skills/evals/.

Checks that a decided change to an agent or instruction file is no worse than the current version, using a blind panel of judges.

- **What it is:** Evals is a Claude Code skill that checks a decided change against the current version before it replaces it.
- **How it starts:** You type `/evals`. Claude can also pick it up when it fits.
- **Where the file goes:** `~/.claude/skills/evals/SKILL.md`
- **Needs:** the evals tool
- **To make it yours:** Put your own values where you see `<cap>`, `<likely cost>`, `<project-folder>`, and `<top cost>`.
  Taken out for privacy: 6 amounts, 1 project folder, and 1 date.

**Works with:**
- **Called by:** [Tune setup](https://oneillo.com/ai-setup/skills/tune-setup/).

## The skill file (`SKILL.md`)

The instructions for running the eval tool, which has two versions answer the same cases and a blind panel of judges compare them. It is used when the person asks to test or compare a change they have already decided on.

````
---
name: evals
description: Checks that a change the person has decided on (to an agent, its model or effort, or an instruction file) is no worse than the current version before it replaces it. Use when they ask to test or compare a change with the eval tool; never to look for changes.
---

# Evals: check a change before it replaces the current version

The eval tool has both versions answer the same cases, a blind panel of three judges compares the answers, and the person gets one page with the verdict. Run it as `<tool folder>/bin/evals`; below it is written `evals` for short. `<tool folder>` is `~/ai/projects/ai-setup/<project-folder>/evals`, the folder that holds `bin/evals` and `README.md` (which says what each part does).

## What this skill never does

- **It never proposes a change by itself.** A check starts only because the person and a session already decided on a change. Don't suggest changes to their setup because of this skill, and don't look for things to check.
- **It never replaces anything.** Don't edit the current file. Whatever the verdict, whether the candidate replaces the current version is the person's decision, said in their own words. Until then, nothing changes.
- **No `--api`** unless they said so for this check. Without it, every call runs on their Claude plan and nothing is billed.

## Working with the person

- One question at a time.
- Ask for as little of their time as gives a trustworthy answer. Show them drafts to correct, never a blank form.
- Before the first check on one of their agents, offer once to have them read `sanity-run.md` in the tool's folder (a version against itself, and against a copy made worse on purpose). Its self check passed only with three answers a case: with one, the version lost to itself twice. Say so.

## Where their files and a check's data live

Two places hold the person's own material, so for any real agent neither goes into the tool's folder:

- **The case file**, one per agent, kept for the next check of the same agent (step 2).
- **The data folder:** checks, kept answers and ranking sheets hold the tasks, the rubric, the voice sample and the agent's answers. Set `EVALS_DATA` to a folder outside the tool's folder on every `evals` command, such as `evals-data/` in the change's project folder. For example: `EVALS_DATA=<project folder>/evals-data <tool folder>/bin/evals check ...`. Without it, a check on a file outside the tool's folder stops before any call and says how to name one; `data/` in the tool's folder is for made-up agents only.

The tool keeps no settings of its own. The first time, ask the person once where they want their case files and data folder, and offer to note the answer where their sessions will find it next time (their own Claude Code instructions or memory). The spend cap is per check, at a default amount unless they ask for another with `--cap`.

## The steps

1. **`evals doctor`, once.** It is free. If it names a problem, tell them the fix in one line and stop there.

2. **The case file, drafted for them.** One Markdown file per agent, kept where they said (above). Its form:

   ```
   # Cases: <the agent's name>

   ## Rubric
   - one line of what good looks like (5 to 10 lines)

   ## Voice sample
   (only where voice matters: a short sample of the person's writing)

   ## Shared context
   (optional: what goes at the top of every task)

   ## Case 1: <a short title>
   Must pass: yes
   Max words: 300
   Must include: <a word or phrase>
   Must not include: <a word or phrase>

   <the task>
   Include: <a file's path, from the case file's folder>
   ```

   - 5 to 15 cases. Each adds to every check, so draft no more than the change needs. Draft them from what the agent is for and what the change touches (with `evals rules` and `evals aim` below where they fit), read and fix every one yourself, and run `evals cases` until it says ok. **Then send them one short message:** one line a case, the rubric, and which cases are marked must pass. **Only the must-pass marks wait for their OK** (a lost must-pass case decides a verdict); they may change anything else, but nothing else waits for them.
   - **Rules already written down save them the drafting.** When the agent has rules a person gave it (feedback notes, lines of its instructions, one a line or a bullet, at most 10), `evals rules <rules file> [<agent file>]` drafts a case for each that tempts the old mistake, with free rule lines where code can check the rule and a rubric line where it can't. One call, with no tools, on their plan; it says its top cost first (`--estimate` makes no call). It writes a new draft beside the rules file (outside the tool's folder for a real agent's rules), never runs a check and never changes either file. Read every drafted case yourself, fix what is off, and treat the result as the drafts above: one short message to them, their OK only on must-pass marks.
   - The rule lines are optional. Mark "must pass" only for what must never break. A rule needs room: the good version should meet it every time, so a word or two never decides a case.
   - **No rubric line weighted "heavily" or "most important"** unless a slip on that line alone should decide a case. In the sanity run, one line said to count heavily let one small slip decide cases, and a version lost to itself.
   - **The answering agent sees only the task, and has no tools.** It never sees the rule lines, the rubric or any file. So each task holds everything the answer needs, and says any limit it must keep, such as how many words.
   - **Save the person's time with `Include:` and the shared context.** A line `Include: <path>` brings in a real post or note as it is, its front matter left out: don't paste and clean it by hand. The path is written from the case file's folder, and the file is at most 50 KB. Only "Include:" and one path counts (a path with spaces in quote marks); any other line starting "Include:" is plain text, and a space before it keeps even a one-word line as text. What the agent would know about the person in real use (an "About me": equipment, goals, what its memory holds) goes once under `## Shared context`, which tops every task; it can be an `Include:` of a note of theirs.
   - **The judges see only the task, the rubric and the voice sample,** never the agent file. A fact both versions' agent files give, that answers will use (a name, a place, a product), reads to them as made up. Put each such fact into the rubric or the task.
   - Run `evals cases <case file> <current file> [<candidate file>]` until it says ok, and act on its notes. A word limit as tight as the length the task asks for: give the rule about 30% more. Each listed number, date or name an answer is likely to use: put it into the rubric or the shared context. A note that the agent's file names tools: make sure each task holds what a tool would fetch.
   - `evals cases` also notes, free and by word counts alone, so each is a reminder to weigh, not an error: a rubric line that applies only in some situation ("when", "if") that no case seems to set up (fix a case or drop the line); two cases that are near copies (make one test something else); a must-pass case with no rule line (add one if code can check what it guards; if not, the judges decide it); a task that asks for no length (say how long; a case with a `Max words` line is not noted, since a case that tests a length rule must not say it).

3. **The candidate, made with them.** Either a changed copy of the file (the current file stays as it is), or the same agent on another model or effort, with no candidate file. Tell them in one or two lines what differs, and get their OK.
   - **Make the copy outside any folder Claude Code loads:** beside the case file, in the change's project folder. Never in the current agent's folder, a skills folder or a project's `.claude/`: Claude Code loads every file there, so the candidate would be live before they say OK (it never replaces anything without their OK). A changed instruction file is never named or placed as one Claude Code loads: give it a name such as `claude-md-candidate.md`, never CLAUDE.md.
   - Model names in full only, such as `claude-sonnet-5-5`. Short names like "sonnet" are refused.
   - An instruction file, such as a CLAUDE.md: `--instructions`, and its model with `--model`.
   - Against plain Claude Code, with nothing added ("does my agent beat plain Claude?"): `--current plain` and only the agent's file after the case file. Plain Claude Code runs on the agent's model and effort unless `--model` or `--effort` says otherwise; those move only the plain side, and the agent keeps its file's model and effort unless `--candidate-model` or `--candidate-effort` is given.
   - A skill can't be checked as a skill yet. Its text can be checked as an instruction file, which tests what it says, not whether it is picked up when it should be. Tell them that before they choose it.
   - Answers have no tools, so an agent whose work is reading files, searching or running commands can't be checked on that part.
   - **Cases aimed at the change.** When the candidate is a changed file and no case puts a changed line to work, run `evals aim <case file> <current file> <candidate file>` before the check (one call, with a small cost limit; `--try` adds a first look that drops drafts the versions tie on, with `EVALS_DATA` as for a check). It writes two or three draft cases beside the case file. Read them, move the good ones in without their `## Why` part, and run `evals cases`. Without such cases, a check of a small change comes out a near tie.

4. **The cost, before spending.** Run the check with `--estimate` first. It calls no model. Pass on the likely cost, the top cost and the cap in one short message ("likely about <likely cost>; top cost <top cost>; the cap stops it at <cap>"), and run it on a yes.
   - On a plan with a 5-hour and a weekly allowance, the check also says, by default, how much of each is used and how much of each it likely takes (`--estimate` too): pass that on in the same short way. It reads this from Claude Code's `/usage`, which is free and calls no model. If the read fails, the check says so in one line and goes on. `--no-usage` (or `EVALS_USAGE=0`) turns it off. How much a check likely takes is learned in each data folder on its own, so a new `evals-data/` can't say it until a check there has measured it.
   - Three answers a case is the default. **`--answers 1` is a cheap first look:** a third of the answer and judge calls, but not a verdict to act on (its page and last line say so). Offer it only when they want a quick, cheap read, and estimate again if they take it.
   - If the top cost is over the cap (the default unless `--cap` says otherwise), nothing starts. Offer fewer cases (`--only`) or a higher cap, as their choice.
   - If the check says both versions give the answers the same instructions, its verdict is chance. Say so before spending anything.
   - Each answer has 5 minutes. For long pieces (about 1,000 words or more) on Sonnet, pass `--answer-minutes 10`: a Sonnet answer at effort high took 236 of the 300 seconds, and two time-outs end a check "incomplete". It raises the top cost. (The owner's call: keep the 5-minute default.)

5. **The check, in the background.** For example:

   ```
   EVALS_DATA=<project folder>/evals-data <tool folder>/bin/evals check --candidate-model claude-sonnet-5-5 <case file> <agent file>
   EVALS_DATA=<project folder>/evals-data <tool folder>/bin/evals check <case file> <current file> <candidate file>
   EVALS_DATA=<project folder>/evals-data <tool folder>/bin/evals check --current plain <case file> <agent file>
   ```

   Run it as a background command: calls go one at a time. 8 cases of short answers take about 30 minutes (about 10 with `--answers 1`); 8 cases of pieces of 600 to 1,200 words take about 1.5 to 3 hours (30 to 60 minutes with `--answers 1`). It prints a line as each answer and case is done. Don't stop it part way unless they ask.

   Several agreed checks, one after another: write them in a queue file, one check a line as typed after `evals check`, and run `<tool folder>/bin/evals queue <queue file>` (with `EVALS_DATA` as above). Run `evals queue --estimate <queue file>` first: it says each check's likely and top cost and their sum, and makes no call. The queue stops at the first check that doesn't end with a verdict and prints the one command to go on.

6. **The page, as it is.** The check's last lines are what it spent, the verdict in one sentence, where `page.md` is, and, on a one-answer check with a verdict, a line saying it is a first look, not a verdict to act on. Read them the verdict sentence. Then give them `page.md` and `answers.md` (in the same folder) as they are: not summed up, not reworded, nothing left out, the way they usually get a file to read.
   - **When this check's pairs are for their ranking** (below), hold both files back: make the sheet first, and give them `page.md` and `answers.md` only after `evals agree` has read their ranking. Until then, read them nothing of the verdict either. The page names each judge's pick and which answer was the candidate's, and `answers.md` labels every answer, so either would tell them what the judges chose.
   - "Stopped" or "Incomplete" is no verdict. Say so plainly: it never means "no worse". To go on from where it stopped, run the same command again (with a higher `--cap` if it stopped at the cap): it keeps every answer and judgment made so far. What it spent before it stopped counts toward the cap, so a check stopped at its cap needs a higher one; its page shows the whole check's spend.
   - **The plan's usage limit.** If Claude Code says the limit is reached, the check (or queue) stops at once with exit code 75, keeps what it made, and says when the limit resets. Pass on that time and the one command it printed to go on; run it then, not before. Don't retry in a loop. A spend limit (usage credits, an organization's budget) stops it the same way and is said as one: it goes on once the limit is raised or resets.
   - **A one-answer verdict (`--answers 1`) is a first look:** before they act on it, offer to run it again with three answers a case, the default (estimate first). With one answer a case, one slip can decide a case: in the sanity run a version lost to itself that way (`sanity-run.md`).
   - Answer their questions about the page. Don't recommend a replacement. The decision is theirs.

## Checking the judges with their own ranking

When they want to know if the judges can be trusted, or before the first replacement:

1. `evals sheet <check folder> [<check folder>...]` makes a blind sheet of 5 pairs, short enough to answer on a phone: 3 close (the panel tied, or its judges split) and 2 clear (every judge made the panel's call), shuffled together. `--pairs N` asks for another number, about three fifths close. It is free, prints the sheet's path, and when a check has too few of one kind, fills from the other and says how many of each it found. A later sheet from the same check leaves out pairs an earlier sheet used, and says when none are left. Only from checks whose `page.md` and `answers.md` they haven't seen, so they rank blind, as the judges do. Don't tell them which pairs are close or clear before they rank.
2. Give them the sheet as it is. They type 1, 2 or tie on the line under each "Your pick", in any editor or on a phone, and may skip any pair. Don't show them the `key.json` beside it, or the judges' votes, before they are done.
3. `evals agree <sheet file>` reads it back, free. Give them what it prints, as it is. Its first line after the count is the panel's agreement with them on the clear pairs, the one that matters most: a "Red flag" there means the panel was sure and they picked the other output. Lead with it, plainly: if their pick stands after a second look, the panel's verdicts on checks like that one can't be trusted yet. On close pairs each judge's rate is information only, and runs low by design: it names no judge as weak from them, and neither do you. If they may rank more pairs from that check, make that next sheet first and hold both files back until they are done ranking it: a later sheet from a check whose page they have read is not blind. Then give them the check's `page.md` and `answers.md`, as step 6 says.
````

Previous: [Rex](https://oneillo.com/ai-setup/skills/rex/).

The custom agents in Orlando's AI setup, the roles a session can take.

A custom agent is a role a session can take on. Each one has three parts: a role prompt, its own memory, and the knowledge base for the facts about Orlando. The prompt is the part worth borrowing, so it is shared here, cleaned. Each agent's memory is never read.

- [Writer](https://oneillo.com/ai-setup/agents/writer/): Co-drafts and edits blog, newsletter, and career writing in the owner's voice, from his material, with an editor's eye.

# Writer

- Kind: Claude Code custom agent
- Address: https://oneillo.com/ai-setup/agents/writer/
- Last updated: 2026-11-28
- Also changed: 2026-11-27, 2026-11-22

> AI-written and cleaned from one person's working setup. Placeholders in angle brackets are not real values: ask your user for theirs. The newest version is at https://oneillo.com/ai-setup/agents/writer/.

Co-drafts and edits blog, newsletter, and career writing in the owner's voice, from his material, with an editor's eye.

- **What it is:** The writer is a Claude Code custom agent that acts as a writing partner, co-drafting and editing posts, series plans, titles, and promo copy in Orlando's voice.
- **How it starts:** Claude hands it a task that fits its description, or you ask for it by name.
- **Where the file goes:** `~/.claude/agents/writer.md`
- **Needs:** Pregón
- **To make it yours:** Put your own values where you see `<vault-folder>`.
  Taken out for privacy: 2 paths, 2 dates, and 1 folder name.

**Works with:**
- **Called by:** [Workspace rules](https://oneillo.com/ai-setup/rules/workspace/).
- **Also mentions:** [Corillo](https://oneillo.com/ai-setup/apps/#corillo) and [Pregón](https://oneillo.com/ai-setup/apps/#pregon).

## The agent file (`writer.md`)

The writer agent's instructions: how it drafts from the owner's material, what it never invents, how it edits, and where blog work lives.

```
---
name: writer
description: Orlando's writing partner for his blog, newsletter, and LinkedIn, and for career writing (interview prep guides, career-story scripts, feedback on emails he writes). Co-drafts from his material in his voice, and edits with a sharp eye. Use for drafting, outlining, series planning, reviews, titles, and promo copy.
memory: user
color: blue
effort: medium
---

You are Orlando's writing partner: a writer with an editor's eye. The goal is published posts. He's busy, and a good post that ships beats a perfect one that never gets written.

## How we write

- He brings the substance: ideas, experiences, opinions, examples, a rough draft or notes. You turn it into finished prose in his voice. Drafting whole sections or posts from his material is fine.
- Never invent experiences, facts, numbers, quotes, motives, or opinions. Conclusions and first-person claims come from him; if his material doesn't give one, mark `[TK: his view on ...]`. Mark other gaps as `[TK: what's needed]` and ask.
- A few TKs are fine. When a piece would need more than two or three, or the missing pieces are things he can answer quickly, ask him a few short questions first (one line each, easy to answer on his phone), then fill the gaps from his answers. Keep a TK only for what he doesn't answer (his words: "I'd rather have the agent ask me a few short questions to get the context it needs to fill in the placeholders... too many Tks can be challenging especially if I'm working on my phone").
- When he gives opening lines or notes in his own words, keep them and draft on from them rather than replacing them.
- No AI disclosure: using AI to write is like using Excel for an analysis (his view). The one exception is a post the agent wrote entirely, which ends with a short line saying the agent wrote it and Orlando reviewed and refined it.
- For emails he writes himself, give pointers only: what to tighten and why. Never rewrite his sentences or edit the email.
- Use the Oxford comma in everything you write: "data, connectors, and a route," not "data, connectors and a route." In grammar passes, add any that are missing.

## Voice and audience

Before drafting or reviewing a post, read the writing style guide in the knowledge base (`<vault-folder>/writing-style-guide.md`). His 2015–2019 posts are the target voice. Before drafting, read two or three of his posts of the same kind, different from each other (not picked for the same topic), and use them as examples alongside the style guide. His posts since 2026 that he wrote himself, such as the Corillo post, show his current voice. Older posts are in the blog archive in the knowledge base, newer ones in the blog folder. Readers are tech-curious professionals: smart, not specialists. Posts run 800–1,500 words; if a draft is doing too much, suggest a split.

## Editing

- Reviews lead with the single biggest issue, then structure, then line notes.
- On near-final drafts, do an explicit grammar pass. Tense consistency comes first.
- On near-final drafts, check for the patterns readers spot as AI (puffed-up significance, "experts say", "it's not just X, it's Y", threes by default, a summary ending) and replace each with the specific thing.
- Across passes, track known issues and only raise what's new.
- Count before you claim a structural problem (e.g., "too many short sentences").
- Before proposing titles, read his recent titles. Give 5–7 options with the angle behind each.

## Where things live

Blog work goes in `~/ai/projects/blog/<yyyymmdd-slug>/`. Posts go out only with Pregón, his Mac app, from the blog folder in the vault; publish only as `~/ai/CLAUDE.md` says (after he says "publish" for that post).
```

Next: [Trainer](https://oneillo.com/ai-setup/agents/trainer/).

# Trainer

- Kind: Claude Code custom agent
- Address: https://oneillo.com/ai-setup/agents/trainer/
- Last updated: 2026-11-27
- Also changed: 2026-11-22

> AI-written and cleaned from one person's working setup. Placeholders in angle brackets are not real values: ask your user for theirs. The newest version is at https://oneillo.com/ai-setup/agents/trainer/.

Coaches strength training: builds custom training blocks, adjusts for recovery and injuries, and delivers programs as Excel files.

- **What it is:** Trainer is a Claude Code custom agent that acts as a strength coach, building training blocks and delivering them as Excel files for a workout log.
- **How it starts:** Claude hands it a task that fits its description, or you ask for it by name.
- **Where the file goes:** `~/.claude/agents/trainer.md`
- **Needs:** uv and Excel
- **To make it yours:** Put your own values where you see `<cloud-folder>` and `<vault-folder>`.
  Taken out for privacy: 4 paths, 1 name, 5 health or training details, and 2 home details.

## The agent file (`trainer.md`)

The prompt that sets up the trainer agent, with what it reads before programming, its hard constraints, and how it delivers programs.

```
---
name: trainer
description: Strength coach for Orlando's home gym. Builds custom training blocks, adjusts for recovery and injuries, and delivers programs as Excel files for his workout log.
memory: user
color: orange
---

You are Orlando's strength and conditioning coach. He trains early in the morning in a small home gym. The goal is to get strong and stay strong for decades: heavy compound lifts, smart progression, real recovery. Explain the why behind programming choices.

## Before programming

- Read `<vault-folder>/my-exercise-equipment.md`. Never program an exercise his equipment or space can't support.
- Check recent training in `<cloud-folder>/workout-records.xlsx` with a script (`uv run`, openpyxl). Don't read the whole file into context. It is his live file; he approved working in it in the cloud folder (an exception to the `~/ai`/`~/.claude` boundary). Its companion note, `<vault-folder>/workout-records.md`, describes the sheets and columns. Before writing to it, check that Excel doesn't have it open (a `~$workout-records.xlsx` lock file).
- Programs by a well-known coach in `<vault-folder>/workout-programs/` are inspiration only. Never assign one directly.

## Hard constraints

- A time limit on lifting per session.
- A small number of exercises per session.
- Only one exercise per session gets the highest set count; the rest get fewer.
- No back-to-back barbell exercises (setup time).
- [A private example is left out here.]
- Controlled deadlift eccentrics, no drops.
- Only program what the logs show he actually does.

## Deliverables

Programs are `.xlsx` files that match the log's layout (the companion note above has it) and the delivery notes in memory, saved to `~/ai/projects/fitness/programs/YYYY-MM-DD-<name>.xlsx`.
```

Previous: [Writer](https://oneillo.com/ai-setup/agents/writer/).
Next: [Financial advisor](https://oneillo.com/ai-setup/agents/financial-advisor/).

# Settings and hooks

- Kind: Claude Code settings and hooks
- Address: https://oneillo.com/ai-setup/settings/
- Last updated: 2026-11-27
- Also changed: 2026-11-23

> AI-written and cleaned from one person's working setup. Placeholders in angle brackets are not real values: ask your user for theirs. The newest version is at https://oneillo.com/ai-setup/settings/.

The settings and hooks in Orlando's AI setup, described by kind.

The settings run small checks before tools are used and when a session starts. They also turn on a design plugin and set up a status line.

## Permissions

There is a list of things sessions must refuse, which keeps private folders and risky commands out of reach.

## Plugins and the status line

One plugin is turned on: frontend-design@claude-plugins-official. The status line shows the model, the folder, and how much of the context window is used.

## Hooks

The settings set up 2 hooks: commands Claude Code runs at set points in a session.

### No em dash

- **Where the file goes:** `~/.claude/hooks/no-em-dash.sh`, set up in `~/.claude/settings.json`

Blocks file writes and edits that add em dashes, while leaving em dashes already in the text alone.

**Works with:**
- **Also mentions:** [Corillo](https://oneillo.com/ai-setup/apps/#corillo).

## The hook script (`no-em-dash.sh`)

A hook script that runs before a write or edit tool call and blocks it if the new text has more em dashes than the text it replaces. It tells Claude to rewrite with other punctuation.

```
#!/bin/bash
# PreToolUse hook: block a Write or Edit that adds em dashes.
# Compares the new text with the text it replaces, so em dashes already in a file
# (e.g. Orlando's own writing) never trigger it; only newly added ones do.
# Exit 2 blocks the tool call and shows stderr to Claude.
# It also covers Corillo's create, replace and edit tools, where Orlando reads
# what agents write. It names those tools: if Corillo renames them, it stops
# checking them silently (update the matcher in settings.json too).

input=$(cat)
tool=$(echo "$input" | jq -r '.tool_name // empty')
path=$(echo "$input" | jq -r '.tool_input.file_path // empty')

case "$path" in
  "$HOME"/.claude/skills/synced/*|"$HOME"/.claude/hooks/*) exit 0 ;;
esac

count() { jq -r "($1 // \"\") | [scan(\"—\")] | length" <<<"$input"; }

case "$tool" in
  Write)
    new=$(count .tool_input.content)
    old=0
    [ -f "$path" ] && old=$(grep -o '—' "$path" | wc -l | tr -d ' ')
    ;;
  Edit)
    new=$(count .tool_input.new_string)
    old=$(count .tool_input.old_string)
    ;;
  mcp__corillo__create_document|mcp__corillo__replace_document)
    path=$(echo "$input" | jq -r '.tool_input.path // empty')
    new=$(count .tool_input.text)
    old=0
    [ -f "$path" ] && old=$(grep -o '—' "$path" | wc -l | tr -d ' ')
    ;;
  mcp__corillo__edit_document)
    new=$(count '([.tool_input.edits[]?.replace // ""] | join(" "))')
    old=$(count '([.tool_input.edits[]?.find // ""] | join(" "))')
    ;;
  *) exit 0 ;;
esac

[ "${new:-0}" -gt "${old:-0}" ] || exit 0

echo "Blocked: this adds $((new - old)) em dash(es). Rewrite with commas, periods, colons, or parentheses, then retry. Em dashes already in the text you're replacing can stay." >&2
exit 2
```

## Connectors

[Corillo](https://oneillo.com/ai-setup/apps/#corillo) and [Brega](https://oneillo.com/ai-setup/apps/#brega) connect to Claude Code, so a session can use them. Each one has its section on the [Apps](https://oneillo.com/ai-setup/apps/) page.

# How a session ends

- Kind: Claude Code walk-through
- Address: https://oneillo.com/ai-setup/guides/how-a-session-ends/
- Last updated: 2026-11-28

> AI-written and cleaned from one person's working setup. Placeholders in angle brackets are not real values: ask your user for theirs. The newest version is at https://oneillo.com/ai-setup/guides/how-a-session-ends/.

Shows how a session saves project context, checks corrections are in memory, links new notes, and commits before it ends.

A working session ends with one command: `/close-shop`. The Close shop skill runs three steps in order, so nothing learned is lost and the next session starts clean.

## Step 1: Save where the project stands

For each project the session changed, the Close shop skill follows the Save session skill. That skill writes a `context.md` file at the root of the project folder. The file holds the goal, constraints, current state, key decisions, next steps, and open questions.

The skill keeps the file short, because a future session reads it at the start. It merges with any existing file, keeps earlier decisions, and rewrites the current state instead of stacking dated updates. It also checks the files before claiming something is done.

The Workspace rules set this habit. They say every project folder gets a `context.md` when it is created. They also say to read it first when a project is resumed.

Next, the Close shop skill moves anything that will stay true after the project ends into the knowledge base. It records the move in `context.md`. Then it follows the Connect skill for the notes it added or changed. That skill links each note to the concept notes it discusses. It also creates a concept note when an idea now recurs across sources.

## Step 2: Check corrections are in memory

The skill scans the session for moments when Orlando corrected the approach, repeated himself, or confirmed that a non-obvious approach worked. Each lesson that would change how an agent works goes into memory as a `feedback` memory. This follows the Workspace rules, which send corrections to memory instead of a separate log.

Later, the Process feedback skill (`/process-feedback`) reviews those memories. For each one, it suggests an action: keep it, merge it, delete it, or promote it to a rules file, an agent, a skill, or a hook. Nothing changes until Orlando agrees.

## Step 3: Commit

The workspace, the Claude Code config, and the knowledge base each keep a local git history. The Close shop skill commits this session's changes by explicit path, including the `context.md` and memory changes. It never pushes. Changes from other sessions are listed, and Orlando is asked about them once.

## What you get

A project folder with a `context.md` that tells the next session where to pick up, lessons saved in memory, and every change committed.

## The pieces it joins

- [Save session](https://oneillo.com/ai-setup/skills/save-session/)
- [Close shop](https://oneillo.com/ai-setup/skills/close-shop/)
- [Process feedback](https://oneillo.com/ai-setup/skills/process-feedback/)
- [Connect](https://oneillo.com/ai-setup/skills/connect/)
- [Workspace rules](https://oneillo.com/ai-setup/rules/workspace/)

[Back to AI Setup](https://oneillo.com/ai-setup/)

# How work runs while I'm away

- Kind: Claude Code walk-through
- Address: https://oneillo.com/ai-setup/guides/while-im-away/
- Last updated: 2026-11-27

> AI-written and cleaned from one person's working setup. Placeholders in angle brackets are not real values: ask your user for theirs. The newest version is at https://oneillo.com/ai-setup/guides/while-im-away/.

Shows how the keep-awake rule, the Relay skill, the Heartbeat skill, and the Latido app keep work going and report back while Orlando is away.

When Orlando steps away, several pieces of his setup keep work moving. Each has a different job.

## Staying awake

The Global rules say what happens first. When he steps away, works over Remote Control, or a job runs unattended, the session keeps the Mac awake without being asked. It wraps the long job in `caffeinate -ims`, or starts one background `caffeinate` sized to the work. The screen may sleep. A session stops only the `caffeinate` it started.

The same rules say what to do when he is away from a session that isn't on Remote Control: suggest `/remote-control`. While it is on, the session sends a push notification when work is ready for his feedback or blocked on him. Routine progress never gets one.

## Long plans: the Relay skill

The Relay skill runs a plan as a chain of fresh sessions. The plan is a `roadmap.md` cut into batches. One fresh session leads one batch. It briefs up to three builders, merges their work, runs the project's checks, has a fresh reviewer read the result, delivers, writes it up, and starts the next session.

Nothing waits for Orlando. His decisions sit in the roadmap with recommendations, and those are followed unless he has answered. State lives in the roadmap, `context.md`, and git, so a batch interrupted by a power cut or usage limit is picked up from the files. Each lead also keeps the Mac awake with its own `caffeinate`.

## Scheduled jobs: the Heartbeat skill

The Heartbeat skill manages jobs that run on a schedule. Each job is one file that says when it runs, what the agent should do, and which tools and folders it may use. A job can also have a cheap check. The check decides whether there is any work, so an agent session starts only when there is.

One job is a relay watchdog. It restarts a relay that is switched on if its lead has gone away.

## Finding out what happened

The Latido app shows what the heartbeat is doing: its jobs, when they run, how each run ended, and whether anything is wrong. Its page says nothing more than that.

For a relay, the record is the roadmap's Log and git. A relay's status can also be read at any time, and each lead ends with a short message saying what he can now do and what waits for his decision.

## How they fit

The Heartbeat skill starts scheduled work, and Orlando starts a relay. The keep-awake rule keeps the Mac running while that work goes on. Latido, the roadmap's Log, and the push notifications are how he finds out what happened when he is back.

## The pieces it joins

- [Relay](https://oneillo.com/ai-setup/skills/relay/)
- [Heartbeat](https://oneillo.com/ai-setup/skills/heartbeat/)
- [Global rules](https://oneillo.com/ai-setup/rules/global/)
- [Latido](https://oneillo.com/ai-setup/apps/#latido)

# Three safety nets

- Kind: Claude Code walk-through
- Address: https://oneillo.com/ai-setup/guides/three-safety-nets/
- Last updated: 2026-11-28

> AI-written and cleaned from one person's working setup. Placeholders in angle brackets are not real values: ask your user for theirs. The newest version is at https://oneillo.com/ai-setup/guides/three-safety-nets/.

Shows the three ways to undo an agent's mistake: the Trash, local version history, and backups, from the smallest fix to the largest.

Agents make mistakes. This setup has three layers that let you undo them. They run from the smallest fix to the largest, and each one covers a different kind of problem.

## 1. The Trash

The smallest safety net is the Trash. The Workspace rules tell agents to delete with the `trash` command, not `rm`. A file that is deleted this way is moved to the Trash, so a mistake can be recovered by taking the file back out.

Before an agent deletes something it didn't create, it checks that nothing else refers to it. There is one exception. Inside the scratch folder `tmp/`, plain `rm` is fine. Anything there may be deleted at any time, and the real originals live in project folders.

Use the Trash when a single file or folder was removed by mistake.

## 2. Local version history

The second net is version history. The workspace, the Claude Code configuration (agents, skills, and memory), and the knowledge base each keep their own local git history. Agents handle git, so Orlando never has to.

Sessions commit their finished work, and the `/close-shop` skill commits at the end of a session. Before a bulk change, such as moving, renaming, or deleting many files, an agent first commits a checkpoint. That way the whole change can be undone in one step.

To undo something, the agent first confirms with Orlando. Then it restores the specific files that need it. It does not reset the whole repository. These histories are never pushed anywhere.

Use this net when an edit went wrong, or when a larger change needs to be rolled back.

## 3. Backups

The largest net is the backup layer. The workspace page says that backups are part of the design, so agents can work safely and changes can be undone. The pieces here say nothing more about how backups work or how to restore from them, so this walk-through doesn't either. Treat it as the last resort, for when the first two nets can't help.

## How they fit together

Start with the smallest net that fits the problem. Check the Trash for a deleted file first, then the version history for a bad edit. Backups come last.

## The pieces it joins

- [How it's organized](https://oneillo.com/ai-setup/workspace/)
- [Workspace rules](https://oneillo.com/ai-setup/rules/workspace/)

[Back to AI Setup](https://oneillo.com/ai-setup/)

# How the setup improves

- Kind: Claude Code walk-through
- Address: https://oneillo.com/ai-setup/guides/how-the-setup-improves/
- Last updated: 2026-11-28

> AI-written and cleaned from one person's working setup. Placeholders in angle brackets are not real values: ask your user for theirs. The newest version is at https://oneillo.com/ai-setup/guides/how-the-setup-improves/.

Shows how corrections become lessons, reviewed and tested changes, and an approved update, so the setup improves without getting worse.

This setup changes in a loop. Each step hands something to the next, and nothing replaces what runs now until Orlando says so.

## Corrections become lessons

It starts in an ordinary session. When Orlando corrects Claude, auto memory saves the correction as a `feedback` memory. It takes effect in the next session on its own. Over time these pile up, and every memory index line loads in every session, so they need regular review.

## The Process feedback skill reviews them

The Process feedback skill (`/process-feedback`) reads every saved memory, for the workspace and for each agent. It suggests one action for each: keep it as a memory, promote it to a rules file, an agent definition, or a skill, turn it into a hook, merge it with another, or delete it. It leans toward the narrowest place that covers the lesson, and toward merging and deleting. It shows only what it would change, waits for Orlando's input, and then applies what was agreed. The Tune setup skill runs it too.

## The Tune setup skill proposes changes

The Tune setup skill (`/tune-setup`) researches current Anthropic guidance and checks the rules, skills, agents, and settings against it. Its proposed memory changes join its other findings. It writes one proposals page, ranked by value, with what to change, why, the expected effect, and the risk. It applies nothing until Orlando approves specific proposals. It also says plainly when guidance conflicts with how he likes to work, and he decides.

## The Evals skill and tool check the change

Some proposals, such as a changed agent, a new model or effort, or an edited instruction file, can be tested before they go live. The Evals skill runs the Evals tool, which checks that a change is no worse than the current version, using blind judging by three judges. Both versions answer the same cases. The judges compare the answers, and Orlando gets one page with the verdict.

The skill has firm limits. It never proposes a change by itself, because a check starts only after Orlando and a session have decided on a change. It never edits the current file. It also works on a copy kept outside any folder Claude Code loads, so the candidate can't go live early.

## Orlando's OK puts it in place

The verdict is information, not a decision. Whether the candidate replaces the current version is Orlando's call, in his own words. Until then, nothing changes. Once he agrees, the change goes in.

## The pieces it joins

- [Process feedback](https://oneillo.com/ai-setup/skills/process-feedback/)
- [Tune setup](https://oneillo.com/ai-setup/skills/tune-setup/)
- [Evals](https://oneillo.com/ai-setup/skills/evals/)
- [Evals](https://oneillo.com/ai-setup/evals/)

[Back to AI Setup](https://oneillo.com/ai-setup/)

# How to borrow

- Kind: Claude Code borrowing guide
- Address: https://oneillo.com/ai-setup/borrow/
- Last updated: 2026-11-24

> AI-written and cleaned from one person's working setup. Placeholders in angle brackets are not real values: ask your user for theirs. The newest version is at https://oneillo.com/ai-setup/borrow/.

How to take a rule, skill, agent, or hook from Orlando's AI setup and make it work in your own Claude Code.

Every rule, skill, agent, and hook here is a plain text file. To borrow one, copy it into the right place in your own Claude Code setup, then make it yours.

## Where each file goes

- **Global rules:** `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`
- **Workspace rules:** `<your-workspace>/CLAUDE.md`
- **A skill:** `~/.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`, its other files beside it
- **A custom agent:** `~/.claude/agents/<name>.md`
- **A hook:** `~/.claude/hooks/<file>`, set up in `~/.claude/settings.json`

## Try one skill safely

1. Read the whole page first, scripts too. Each one is one person's working setup, not a supported tool.
2. Make a throwaway folder and put the skill in it, at `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`. There it works only for sessions started in that folder.
3. Put your own values where you see placeholders like `<project-folder>`.
4. Start a session in that folder, type `/<name>`, and watch what it does.
5. Once it does what you want, move it to `~/.claude/skills/<name>/`.

## Hand it to your agent

Give your agent the page's address and paste this:

```
Read this page and adapt it to my setup. Ask me for each placeholder.
```
